Methodology

      
The problem. The USGS Protected Areas Database (PAD-US) is the best available inventory of U.S. public and protected land, but it was never designed for clean acreage accounting: its feature classes overlap, parcels appear in multiple layers, and attributes frequently conflict. Summing it naively overcounts land by millions of acres.

      
Overlap resolution

      
PAD-US Fee parcels are treated as authoritative. Military and tribal lands from the Proclamation layer, and conservation easements from the National Conservation Easement Database (NCED), are added only where they do not intersect Fee parcels — a pairwise erase-then-merge sequence that prioritizes recorded fee ownership. Designation parcels are excluded entirely: quality control (verified against the Montana Cadastral Framework) showed many are privately held land.

      
Owner reclassification

      
A Python decision tree evaluates each parcel's Category, Owner Type, Owner Name, Manager Name, Designation Type, and local-description fields to assign one of twelve EPS ownership classes, with researched special-case logic separating state trust lands from other state lands (local designation text, state-specific rules, and manager attributes). Try it on the Owner classifier tab.

      
Water masking & area accounting

      
County land area was derived by extracting open-water classes from NLCD (Lower 48, Alaska) and NOAA C-CAP high-resolution land cover (Hawaii) — about 38 GB of rasters converted to polygons and erased from county boundaries — so ownership percentages reference land, not total area. The dissolved ownership layer was intersected with water-erased county boundaries in three equal-area projections (CONUS, Alaska, and Hawaii Albers) and tabulated by county GEOID. Private land is computed as land area minus all public and conservation categories.

      
Validation

      
Results were reconciled against the prior 2019 EPS analysis, the Congressional Research Service's federal land report (R42346), and state land board records. Every national-level shift over two percent was explained — including a 2.85-million-acre error discovered in the 2019 study's Minnesota state trust figures.
